content: The text provided is a list of references from various studies, articles, and reports related to HIV prevention, treatment, and outcomes, particularly focusing on mother-to-child transmission, antiretroviral therapy (ART), and public health strategies. 1. Pulerwitz and Bongartz (2014) emphasized the critical role of addressing stigma in achieving an AIDS-free future, as published in The Lancet Global Health. 2. The Sustainable East Africa Research in Community Health (SEARCH) initiative provides valuable insights into community health interventions, with its website accessed on August 25, 2015. 3. The Max ART Project, based in Victoria, Canada, focuses on innovative communication strategies for HIV prevention, with its website accessed on August 25, 2015. 4. The Botswana Combination Prevention Project (BCPP) explores integrated approaches to HIV prevention, with its website accessed on August 25, 2015. 5. The HPTN 071 (PopART) study investigates the impact of combination prevention strategies on HIV incidence, with its website accessed on August 25, 2015. 6. The ANRS 12249 TasP Protocol outlines a trial on treatment as prevention (TasP) for HIV, with the protocol document accessed on August 25, 2015. 7. The Global Plan to eliminate new HIV infections among children by 2015 and keep their mothers alive (2011–2015) highlights international efforts to reduce mother-to-child transmission, with resources accessed on August 25, 2015. 8. Azman et al. (2015) conducted a systematic review comparing Option B+ and Option B for improving outcomes in HIV-infected women and their infants, with findings accessed on February 8, 2016. 9. The Kesho Bora Study Group (2011) compared triple antiretroviral therapy with zidovudine and single-dose nevirapine prophylaxis during pregnancy and breastfeeding to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV-1, as published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases. 10. The Kesho Bora Study Group (2012) further analyzed maternal HIV-1 disease progression 18–24 months post-delivery based on different antiretroviral prophylaxis regimens, as reported in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 11. Shapiro et al. (2010) evaluated antiretroviral regimens during pregnancy and breastfeeding in Botswana, with results published in The New England Journal of Medicine. 12. Shapiro et al. (2013) assessed HIV transmission and 24-month survival in a randomized trial of HAART to prevent mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy and breastfeeding in Botswana, as published in AIDS. 13. Minnear et al. (2013) examined outcomes in Kenyan women who discontinued maternal triple-antiretroviral regimens initially used to prevent mother-to-child transmission, as reported in PLOS One. 14. Okonji et al. (2012) studied CD4, viral load response, and adherence among antiretroviral-naive breastfeeding women receiving triple antiretroviral prophylaxis in Kisumu, Kenya, as published in JAIDS. 15. Thomas et al. (2011) conducted the Kisumu Breastfeeding Study, a clinical trial on triple-antiretroviral prophylaxis to prevent mother-to-child HIV transmission through breastfeeding, as reported in PLOS Medicine. 16. Ayuo et al. (2013) analyzed adherence to and completion of combination antiretroviral therapy for preventing mother-to-child transmission in western Kenya, as published in The Journal of the International AIDS Society. 17. Ekouevi et al. (2012) investigated maternal CD4+ cell count decline after interrupting antiretroviral prophylaxis for preventing mother-to-child transmission, as reported in PLOS One. 18. Gartland et al. (2013) evaluated the field effectiveness of combination antiretroviral prophylaxis for preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission in rural Zambia, as published in AIDS. 19. Giuliano et al. (2013) assessed maternal and infant outcomes two years after delivery in Malawi, focusing on maternal antiretroviral therapy for preventing mother-to-child transmission, as reported in PLOS One. 20. Linguissi et al. (2012) studied the efficiency of HAART in preventing mother-to-child HIV-1 transmission at Saint Camille Medical Centre in Burkina Faso, as published in Asian Pacific Journal of Tropical Medicine. 21. Liotta et al. (2013) reported on the reduction of maternal mortality with HAART in a large cohort of HIV-infected pregnant women in Malawi and Mozambique, as published in PLOS One. 22. Phillips et al. (2014) examined disengagement from antiretroviral therapy services among HIV-positive pregnant and postpartum women in a cohort study, as reported in The Journal of the International AIDS Society. 23. Thistle et al. (2011) evaluated the use of HAART for preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission in rural Zimbabwe during a socioeconomic crisis, as published in Medicine, Conflict, and Survival. 24. Ngemu et al. (2014) assessed the effectiveness of Option B+ HAART for preventing mother-to-child transmission in pregnant HIV-positive women, as reported in BMC Research Notes. 25. Nyandiko et al. (2010) analyzed outcomes of HIV-exposed children in western Kenya, focusing on the efficacy of prevention of mother-to-child transmission in resource-constrained settings, as published in JAIDS. 26. Palombi et al. (2014) studied viro-immunological responses and resistance emergence in HIV-infected women receiving combination antiretroviral regimens for preventing mother-to-child transmission in Malawi, as reported in The Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy. 27. Kamuyango et al. (2014) reviewed one-year outcomes of women starting antiretroviral therapy during pregnancy before and after implementing Option B+ in Malawi, as published in World Journal of AIDS. 28. Kim et al. (2015) analyzed the impact of Option B+ on the antenatal PMTCT cascade in Lilongwe, Malawi, as reported in JAIDS. 29. Lu et al. (2015) studied retention among HIV-infected pregnant women initiating lifelong antiretroviral treatment (Option B+) in Haiti, as presented at the Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections. 30. Namukwaya et al. (2013) shared early challenges faced by women refusing Option B+ drugs in Uganda, as presented at the 7th International AIDS Society Conference. 31. Price et al. (2014) evaluated the uptake of PMTCT using Option B+ in northern rural Malawi, as reported in Sexually Transmitted Infections. 32. Speight et al. (2013) documented the first 18 months of implementing Option B+ for PMTCT at Bwaila Maternity Unit in Lilongwe, as presented at the 7th International AIDS Society Conference. 33. Tweya et al. (2014) explored factors, outcomes, and reasons for loss to follow-up among women in the Option B+ PMTCT program in Lilongwe, Malawi, as published in Tropical Medicine & International Health. 34. Pilotte (2011) analyzed maternal outcomes after HAART for preventing mother-to-child transmission in HIV-infected women in Brazil, as reported in Antiretroviral Therapy. 35. Giuliano et al. (2016) studied retention, transfer out, and loss to follow-up two years after delivery in a cohort of HIV-positive pregnant women in Malawi, as published in International Journal of STD & AIDS. 36. Clouse et al. (2013) examined loss to follow-up before and after delivery among women testing HIV-positive during pregnancy in Johannesburg, South Africa, as reported in Tropical Medicine & International Health. 37. De Walque (2007) analyzed sero-discordant couples in five African countries and their implications for prevention strategies, as published in Population and Development Review. 38. The Kenya AIDS Indicator Survey (2012) provided comprehensive data on HIV prevalence and related indicators, with the report accessed on October 27, 2015. 39. WHO's technical update on the use of efavirenz during pregnancy highlighted its public health implications, with the document accessed on October 16, 2015. 40. O’Brien et al. (2014) evaluated the incremental cost of switching from Option B to Option B+ for PMTCT, as published in Bulletin of the World Health Organization. 41. Gopalappa et al. (2014) analyzed the costs and benefits of Option B+ for PMTCT, as reported in AIDS. 42. Ishikawa et al. (2014) assessed the health outcomes and cost impact of the 2013 WHO guidelines on PMTCT in Zambia, as published in PLOS One. 43. Ngarina et al. (2014) explored women’s preferences regarding infant or maternal antiretroviral prophylaxis for PMTCT during breastfeeding in Tanzania, as reported in PLOS One. 44. Hsieh et al. (2014) summarized community and service provider views to inform the 2013 WHO consolidated antiretroviral guidelines, as published in AIDS. 45. Myer et al. (2015) documented the evolution of antiretroviral therapy services for HIV-infected pregnant women in Cape Town, South Africa, as reported in JAIDS. 46. Phillips et al. (2015) analyzed postpartum transfer of care among HIV-infected women initiating antiretroviral therapy during pregnancy, as published in JAIDS. 47. Woldesenbet et al. (2015) identified missed opportunities along the PMTCT service cascade in South Africa, as reported in PLOS One. 48. Global health estimates (2013) provided data on DALYs, YLLs, and YLDs by cause, age, and sex, with the summary tables accessed on August 25, 2015. 49. WHO's report on adolescent health (2015) emphasized the importance of addressing health challenges in the second decade of life, with the document accessed on August 25, 2015. 50. Auld et al. (2014) compared ART enrollment characteristics and outcomes among HIV-infected adolescents and young adults versus older adults in seven African countries, as reported in MMWR. 51. Lamb et al. (2014) highlighted high attrition rates before and after ART initiation among youth aged 15–24 enrolled in HIV care, as published in AIDS. 52. Grimsrud et al. (2014) analyzed outcomes of ART over a 10-year period in African and Asian HIV programs, as reported in JAIDS. 53. The report Lost in Transitions (2015) addressed challenges faced by adolescents living with HIV in the Asia-Pacific region, with the document accessed on October 31, 2015. 54. Mavhu et al. (2013) explored psychosocial support for HIV-positive adolescents in Harare, Zimbabwe, as reported in PLOS One. 55. Denison et al. (2015) examined adherence to ART and HIV self-management among adolescents living with HIV and their caregivers, as published in The Journal of the International AIDS Society. 56. WHO's guidance on HIV testing and care for adolescents living with HIV (2015) provided recommendations for a public health approach, with the document accessed on August 25, 2015. 57. Siegfried et al. (2013) reviewed the optimal timing for initiating ART in HIV-infected, treatment-naive children aged 2–5 years, as reported in The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 58. Anglemyer et al. (2016) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on universal ART for asymptomatic adults and adolescents with HIV-1 infection and CD4+ T-cell counts ≥500 cells/µl, with findings accessed on February 8, 2016. 59. The IeDEA and COHERE collaborations (2016) analyzed when to start ART for children and adolescents using causal modeling from Africa and Europe, with findings accessed on February 8, 2016. 60. Picat et al. (2014) predicted long-term CD4 reconstitution patterns in HIV-infected children starting ART in sub-Saharan Africa, as reported in a cohort-based modeling study.
